Empirical orthogonal functions of a space-time matrix

Source: R/eofst.R
eofst.Rd

eofst() decomposes a matrix of counts or rates, one row per period and one column per place, into empirical orthogonal functions (EOFs): spatial patterns (the columns of eofs) whose weights over time (the principal component series, the columns of pcs) reproduce the centred matrix, ordered by the share of its variance each explains. A leading pattern that loads on a cluster of places, with a series that rises, is a hot spot that grows; a second pattern of opposite signs is a shift of crime from one set of places to another.

Usage

eofst(z, k = NULL)

# S3 method for class 'eofst'
print(x, ...)

Arguments

z

A numeric matrix (or a data frame of numeric columns) with no missing values: one row per period (at least two), one column per place.

k

NULL (every component) or the most components to keep: one whole number from 1.

x

For print(), an eofst result.

...

Not used by print().

Value

An object of class eofst, a list: eofs (places by components), pcs (periods by components), explained (the share of the variance of each component), sdev and center (the column means taken out).

Details

Each column is centred on its mean over the periods and the centred matrix A is decomposed as A = U D V' (Lorenz 1956; Hannachi, Jolliffe and Stephenson 2007). The EOFs are the columns of V, the series the columns of A V = U D, and explained is d^2 / sum(d^2); sdev is d / sqrt(n - 1), the standard deviation of each series, as stats::prcomp() gives it. An EOF is defined up to its sign: each is signed so that its largest loading in absolute value is positive. The compiled kernel finds V and d from the eigendecomposition (cyclic Jacobi) of the smaller of A'A and A A'; components with d^2 below 1e-10 of the largest are dropped, so a matrix of n periods has at most n - 1 components.

References

Lorenz, E. N. (1956). Empirical Orthogonal Functions and Statistical Weather Prediction. Statistical Forecasting Project, Scientific Report 1. Massachusetts Institute of Technology.

Hannachi, A., Jolliffe, I. T. and Stephenson, D. B. (2007). Empirical orthogonal functions and related techniques in atmospheric science: a review. International Journal of Climatology, 27(9), 1119-1152. doi:10.1002/joc.1499

Examples

set.seed(3)
yr <- 1:10
z <- outer(yr, c(1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0)) + matrix(rnorm(60), 10)
colnames(z) <- paste0("ward", 1:6)
e <- eofst(z)
e
#> eofst: 6 components of 10 periods by 6 places
#>  component   sdev explained cumulative
#>          1 5.8950  0.893300     0.8933
#>          2 1.4340  0.052830     0.9461
#>          3 1.0370  0.027640     0.9737
#>          4 0.7186  0.013270     0.9870
#>          5 0.6166  0.009773     0.9968
#>          6 0.3538  0.003218     1.0000
round(e$eofs[, 1], 2)
#> ward1 ward2 ward3 ward4 ward5 ward6 
#>  0.58  0.57  0.57 -0.05 -0.05  0.03
